                    ### Question
                    A 56-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent retrosternal chest pain. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Endoscopy shows salmon pink mucosa extending 5 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy specimens from the distal esophagus show nonciliated columnar epithelium with numerous goblet cells. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Neoplastic proliferation of esophageal epithelium
opb. Esophageal exposure to gastric acid
opc. Atopic inflammation of the esophagus
opd. Hypermotile esophageal contractions
ope. Fungal infection of the lower esophagus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Esophageal exposure to gastric acid can lead to chronic irritation and metaplasia of the esophageal epithelium, eventually resulting in Barrett's esophagus characterized by salmon pink mucosa with goblet cells. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is esophageal exposure to gastric acid, leading to Barrett's esophagus.
